## 1 Abstract

The sites regression (SREG) model puts the genotype main effects into
the bilinear terms, so its biplot shows which genotypes do best where.
This vignette fits it with the first year as prior, then shows how the
weight of the earlier trial changes the posterior and how WAIC chooses
the number of terms.

## 2 The SREG model with the first year as prior

``` r

fs <-
  bayes_ammi(
      .data       = cultivo2009
    , .y          = y
    , .gen        = entry
    , .env        = site
    , .rep        = rep
    , .nIter      = 3000
    , .prior_data = cultivo2008
    , .n0         = NULL
    , .model      = "SREG"
    , .k          = 2
    , .burnin     = 1000
    , .thin       = 1
    , .chains     = 2
    , .priors     = bys_priors(
          mu_mean     = 0
        , mu_var      = 1e+8
        , tau_mean    = 0
        , tau_var     = 1e+8
        , delta_mean  = 0
        , delta_var   = 1e+8
        , lambda_mean = 0
        , lambda_var  = 1e+8
        , nu          = 1
        , s2          = NULL
        )
    , .level      = 0.95
    , .seed       = 2012
    , .align      = TRUE
    , .waic       = TRUE
    )
fs
```

    Bayesian SREG with 2 multiplicative term(s), an earlier trial as prior (n0 = 3): 12 genotypes, 25 environments, 3 replicates

``` r

bs <-
  bayes_gge_biplot(
      fit           = fs
    , burnin        = 0
    , thin          = 1
    , pb            = 0.05
    , plot_stable   = FALSE
    , plot_unstable = TRUE
    , ncolors       = 5
    , .which        = "both"
    , .grid         = 100
    )
bs$biplot
```

![](data:image/webp;base64,)

On an SREG biplot the first axis reflects mostly the genotype means, so
genotypes far out on it are above or below average rather than
interacting.

## 3 The weight of the earlier trial

`.n0` sets how many observations per cell the earlier trial counts for.
By default it is its number of replicates (3).

``` r

w <- c(0.5, 3, 12)
res <-
  data.table::rbindlist(
      l = lapply(
          X   = w
        , FUN = function(n0) {
            f <-
              bayes_ammi(
                  .data       = cultivo2009
                , .y          = y
                , .gen        = entry
                , .env        = site
                , .rep        = rep
                , .nIter      = 1500
                , .prior_data = cultivo2008
                , .n0         = n0
                , .model      = "AMMI"
                , .k          = 2
                , .burnin     = 500
                , .thin       = 1
                , .chains     = 1
                , .priors     = bys_priors(
                      mu_mean     = 0
                    , mu_var      = 1e+8
                    , tau_mean    = 0
                    , tau_var     = 1e+8
                    , delta_mean  = 0
                    , delta_var   = 1e+8
                    , lambda_mean = 0
                    , lambda_var  = 1e+8
                    , nu          = 1
                    , s2          = NULL
                    )
                , .level      = 0.95
                , .seed       = 4
                , .align      = TRUE
                , .waic       = TRUE
                )
            data.table::data.table(
                n0      = n0
              , mu      = f$summary[parameter == "mu", mean]
              , alpha1  = f$summary[block == "tau", mean][1]
              , lambda1 = f$summary[parameter == "lambda[1]", mean]
              )
          }
        )
    )
res
```

          n0       mu    alpha1  lambda1
       <num>    <num>     <num>    <num>
    1:   0.5 3690.593  484.3266 3602.049
    2:   3.0 3849.168  136.0094 3578.433
    3:  12.0 3980.321 -154.0709 4484.151

As \\n_0\\ grows the posterior moves from the second year (grand mean
3627) towards the first (4069). With \\n_0 = 3\\ it sits halfway. A
small \\n_0\\ is the choice when the earlier trial was grown under
different conditions.

## 4 How many terms?

WAIC compares fits with different numbers of terms (Watanabe 2010;
Vehtari et al. 2017):

``` r

fits <-
  lapply(
      X   = c(1, 2, 3, 5)
    , FUN = function(K) {
        bayes_ammi(
            .data       = cultivo2009
          , .y          = y
          , .gen        = entry
          , .env        = site
          , .rep        = rep
          , .nIter      = 1500
          , .prior_data = cultivo2008
          , .n0         = NULL
          , .model      = "AMMI"
          , .k          = K
          , .burnin     = 500
          , .thin       = 1
          , .chains     = 1
          , .priors     = bys_priors(
                mu_mean     = 0
              , mu_var      = 1e+8
              , tau_mean    = 0
              , tau_var     = 1e+8
              , delta_mean  = 0
              , delta_var   = 1e+8
              , lambda_mean = 0
              , lambda_var  = 1e+8
              , nu          = 1
              , s2          = NULL
              )
          , .level      = 0.95
          , .seed       = 5
          , .align      = TRUE
          , .waic       = TRUE
          )
      }
    )
names(fits) <- paste0("K", c(1, 2, 3, 5))
cp <- do.call(what = bys_compare, args = fits)
cp
```

    Comparison of Bayesian models (smaller is better)

        model terms                  prior      DIC      pD     WAIC  p_waic

    2:     K2     2 earlier trial (n0 = 3) 15493.61 37.4422 15499.51 41.2472
    3:     K3     3 earlier trial (n0 = 3) 15504.81 44.3373 15511.25 48.0848
    4:     K5     5 earlier trial (n0 = 3) 15518.21 56.6405 15524.42 58.8980
            se lambda_last_lower lambda_last_mean   dWAIC dWAIC_se
         <num>             <num>            <num>   <num>    <num>
    1: 50.1988          1863.926         3023.724  0.0000   0.0000
    2: 51.5078          2249.549         3069.854  6.4048   7.3493
    3: 51.6190          1456.046         2366.735 18.1503   8.8759

    Sources: Spiegelhalter et al. (2002); Watanabe (2010); Vehtari et al. (2017).
    Full references: bys_cite(x).

WAIC prefers K1; K2 lie within two standard errors of the difference
(`dWAIC_se`), so the data do not separate them. With the first year as a
strong prior, the singular values of every term are pulled towards that
year’s, and few terms suffice for prediction. The paper chose three
terms with the Bayes factor, which compares the marginal likelihoods of
the models rather than their predictive accuracy.

## 5 References

Perez-Elizalde, S., Jarquin, D. and Crossa, J. (2012). A general
Bayesian estimation method of linear-bilinear models applied to plant
breeding trials with genotype x environment interaction. *Journal of
Agricultural, Biological, and Environmental Statistics*, 17, 15–37.
doi:10.1007/s13253-011-0063-9

Yan, W., Hunt, L. A., Sheng, Q. and Szlavnics, Z. (2000). Cultivar
evaluation and mega-environment investigation based on the GGE biplot.
*Crop Science*, 40(3), 597–605.

Watanabe, S. (2010). Asymptotic equivalence of Bayes cross validation
and widely applicable information criterion in singular learning theory.
*Journal of Machine Learning Research*, 11, 3571–3594.

Vehtari, A., Gelman, A. and Gabry, J. (2017). Practical Bayesian model
evaluation using leave-one-out cross-validation and WAIC. *Statistics
and Computing*, 27(5), 1413–1432.
